item.title: Specialized High School Test Crashes, Rattling Students Across New York
item.description:
Some New York City students hoping to gain entry to one of the city’s exclusive high schools next fall hit a snag on Saturday when the online system used for the admissions test failed.

The Specialized High School Admissions Test, or SHSAT, is the sole admissions criterion for the city’s eight specialized high schools, which include Stuyvesant High School and the Bronx High School of Science.

A note handed to parents who picked up their children from one of the testing sites at Brooklyn Technical High School in Fort Greene said that the “testing sites experienced a technical issue” and so “testing was discontinued.”

The New York City Department of Education later said in a statement that “the vendor experienced technical issue with the testing platform that kept many students from accessing and finishing the test,” and so the exam was rescheduled. The department did not say how many students were affected. Pearson, the vendor of the exam, did not respond to a request for comment.

“Every student who was unable to finish will be automatically rescheduled, and testing on a new date will not affect any student’s score or consideration for admission to a specialized high school,” the statement read. “We apologize for the disruption and are working with the vendor to ensure this is fixed and does not happen again.”

According to the D.O.E., approximately 30,000 eighth graders and 5,000 ninth graders take the test each year. The test went online in 2025, a switch from paper tests, and was scheduled this year for Nov. 14, 15 and 21, as well as an in-school testing day on Nov. 18. It was unclear whether future test days would be affected.

Specialized schools educate only about 5 percent of New York City high schoolers.

“This is a pretty complicated, deep exam and everybody gets psyched for today,” said Gregory Comeau, 67, a New York City tutor who has roughly 25 students taking the SHSAT this year. “It’s an emotional thing, and this has to be a letdown.”

It was unclear how many testing sites were impacted on Saturday and how many students would have to retake the test. According to the note given to parents, students who were scheduled to sit for the exam on Saturday would be given a new testing date by Friday, Nov. 20.

Students who were unable to take the test on Nov. 14 will automatically be rescheduled, while any child who completed testing but felt that it was disrupted by the technical difficulties could request a retest, the note said.

Two years ago, the Panel for Educational Policy, a New York City education group, approved a new five-year, $17 million contract with the education publisher Pearson to administer the SHSAT. The test has been a major point of debate in the city for several years. Some see the exam as an opportunity to attend the city’s best schools, while others view it as a contributing factor to school segregation. During his run for mayor last year, Zohran Mamdani said, “We have the most segregated school system in America,” referring to a 2014 finding from the Civil Rights Project at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Kyisha Brooks-Robinson, 45, said that her daughter, Skyla Robinson, sat down to take the test at Brooklyn Technical High School at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, but the computer took until 10 a.m. to produce the test. She began her math section but was interrupted a short time later when a proctor came in to tell the students in the classroom that they would all be rescheduled.

Ms. Brooks-Robinson said that because Skyla had been able to start the test, her name was designated with an asterisk in the record to ensure she would take an entirely new test the next time around since she got through only two questions.

Skyla was worried that the retake might be harder as a result, her mom said. The rescheduling was also a blow to Skyla, Ms. Brooks-Robinson said, because she had been taking SHSAT study classes twice a week in preparation.

“This test is really stressful for the kids,” Ms. Brooks-Robinson said. “All of the ‘good luck, wish you well, this is going to be a great thing,’ and all of a sudden they cannot take it.”

Ms. Brooks-Robinson said she had suffered outages at work this week when Microsoft went down. That, plus the Federal Aviation Administration’s ground stop on Friday night, made her think the district should be prepared for technical difficulties for the test.

“They should have paper tests on hand, considering everything that is happening,” she said.

Mr. Comeau, the tutor, said that in the competitive environment of specialized high schools in the city, students would roll with the punches of a rescheduled test.

“That’s part of the New York City life,” he said. “Admissions is a nightmare. It’s so unique here the way it works.”

item.title: ‘I Love Being a Girl’: Inside the Life of a Sorority Influencer
item.description:
The Alpha Phi sorority house at the University of Arizona occupies a professionally decorated Spanish colonial-style mansion just off campus. There’s a chandeliered dining room, two pink-and-baby-blue living rooms and a tanning area on the roof.

It’s where Haley DeKreek, a 20-year-old junior, lives with her closest friends. It’s also the backdrop to her budding career. Her work takes place mostly in her room, but she picks up the rewards in the mailroom just off the foyer.

Perpetually suffused with floral perfume, it overflows with packages, many of them hers: boxes with dresses for formals or matching yoga sets, boxes of makeup, hair products and skin care. Some she ordered herself, but many are freebies from brands that have spotted her potential as a TikTok influencer, a one-girl campus marketing powerhouse. Nearly all are destined to appear in the many-stepped “get ready with me” videos she has posted since she was a first-year student rushing sororities.

With more than 45,000 TikTok followers, a gift for self-deprecating humor, a talent manager in Los Angeles and several paid brand deals (the biggest worth $3,000), Ms. DeKreek says she can now pay for all her own shopping, food, vacations and beauty services, just by doing what she has loved since kindergarten, when she played with her mom’s makeup and recorded videos making slime.

She never attends class — not in person, anyway. Her major, retail and consumer science, is entirely online. Apt, given her chosen career path: influencing.

Football players aren’t the only college students who have learned to sell their images for profit. The boom in sorority TikTok videos known as #Rushtok has proved, especially to marketers, that sorority sisters can command audiences all over America.

Ms. DeKreek’s sorority “big,” or mentor, has nearly 800,000 TikTok followers and a Porsche. Sisters at several sororities on Greek Row serve as brand ambassadors, posting about free products and hosting events like yoga on the lawn with the active wear company Alo. On Alpha Phi’s Instagram, the well-known fashion influencers Brigette and Danielle Pheloung visit to promote a “lower sugar” snack, and sorority sisters model brand-sponsored merchandise in posts accompanied by discount codes.

In a recent survey, nearly four in 10 Gen Z respondents said they would take a million social media followers over a steady 9-to-5 job. At several universities, including at the rival Arizona State University, students can now major in content creation.

For Ms. DeKreek, college coursework appears strictly secondary to the business of being @HaleyDeKreek.

In the days before Arizona’s homecoming football game against Iowa State in October, when fraternities and sororities threw events almost every night, I followed her as she drove around Tucson in her cobalt-blue Jeep with oversized wheels, going from beauty appointment to beauty appointment to prepare for the week’s events.

Not that it feels like work. “I love being a girl,” Ms. DeKreek said.

For all that, Ms. DeKreek is ambivalent about social media and the Botox-and-fillers culture she sees on campus — even as her appearance testifies to its pressures, even as she sells products for upholding it.

“People come here and they’re instantly intimidated by the pretty girls,” she said. “They’ll see these videos online, they’ll see the people around them, and instantly start judging themselves.”

She added: “Being a woman in this society is just, like, so overwhelming even compared to five to 10 years ago.”

Wednesday, 1 p.m.: Eyelash lift and tint

Americans have spent the last year agog at male looksmaxxers, who take hammers to their own jaws and inject themselves with dubious substances in the name of beauty. But women have been practicing time-consuming, expensive, invasive and potentially self-destructive interventions for a long, long time. And they’re starting younger than ever.

Twenty-somethings get preventive Botox. Teenagers get fillers. Preteens crowd the aisles of Sephora, purchasing anti-aging serums in bottles the colors of Nerds candy. In a 2025 survey of American plastic surgeons, 57 percent reported that more patients under 30 were requesting cosmetic procedures or injectables. Older women seek to look like young women, and younger women chase the perfected visions of themselves they can generate on their phones.

At 20, Ms. DeKreek said, she has already had lip filler and breast reduction surgery (her large chest made everyday activities physically painful). There have also been multiple rounds of Botox in her forehead (to keep her eyebrows level), cheeks (to stop nighttime jaw-clenching), armpits (to stop sweating) and upper lip (a “lip flip” that bestows a fuller look).

She has a hairstylist for her extensions and a friend who gives her regular spray tans. At home in Folsom, Calif., an affluent Sacramento suburb, she has a therapist and a go-to aesthetician. Today, a Tucson aesthetician gives her an eyebrow-smoothing treatment, and then perma-curls and dyes her lashes in a procedure called a lift and tint.

Ms. DeKreek’s parents sanctioned her procedures, except one injection she got in high school, said her mother, Sandy DeKreek. Then, she thought Haley was too young. Now, proud of her daughter, she says Haley is mature enough to decide.

You hardly have to be an influencer to want to polish your appearance, even if at great effort and cost; being a young woman tends to suffice. For an influencer like Ms. DeKreek, however, beauty draws attention, generating more motivation to be beautiful, encouraging more procedures, which, when posted online, yield money to pay for yet more beauty.

Wednesday, 5 p.m.: Spray tan

Thursday, 8 a.m.: Morning skin care

Ms. DeKreek starts every day by applying six of the many skin care products stored in the white minifridge on her vanity — the first half of her routine.

Thursday, 8:30 a.m.: Wellness walk

Wearing patches to brighten the barely-voting-age skin under their eyes, she and her friend Lea Gorham set off for their morning “wellness walk.”

Ms. DeKreek and her friends gild their days with healthfulness, adopting trends infused with Make America Healthy Again buzzwords. Seed oils and processed foods are out; journaling, early-morning Pilates, protein, probiotics and gut health supplements are in.

As they power-walk through campus, Ms. Gorham debates whether to get lip filler or just a cheaper lip flip. She doesn’t like the way she smiles.

“I don’t necessarily need it, but it’s like, everyone else at this school has it,” she said.

Both procedures are available at a local med spa, where until a couple years ago, undergraduates could use Cat Cash — student bursary funds, generally replenished by parents — to pay for fillers by swiping their student IDs. The spa takes Cat Cash only for non-injectable beauty services now, but lips keep getting flipped.

Thursday, 9:45 a.m.: Morning routine, part 2

Ms. DeKreek begins the second half of her skin care regimen, running a pink electric device over her face, draining her lymph nodes, depuffing invisible puffiness.

To her, beauty helps her feel like her “best self.” Makeup, she said, is like an “art form.”

The most creative and artistic of the four DeKreek sisters, according to her family, Haley began filming videos of herself as a child of 6 or 7, pretending to cook for an audience. She started getting hair highlights in fifth grade. In middle school, she styled her hair for cheerleading competitions and watched hours of YouTube makeup tutorials. In high school, she worked at a hair salon, earning a discount on hair extensions, and taught herself video editing so she could film school football games and other events for student government.

Before rushing sororities, she watched videos for outfit inspiration and tips. With an older sister’s encouragement, she started posting her own rush outfits and makeup routines.

But she’s keenly conscious of social media’s effect on others’ self-esteem. Pushing back in her own small way, she is open about her stubborn acne. She has posted her beauty procedures, not wanting to present her appearance as natural. Having struggled with anxiety and the adjustment to Arizona’s hard-charging party scene her first year of college, she says she wants to post more about mental health.

Thursday, 12 p.m.: Blowout

As Ms. DeKreek fluffs her freshly blow-dried extensions, her hairstylist sets up a tripod to document the final touches. Ms. DeKreek shoots her own videos in the mirror. “You want to post and I’ll repost?” she asks David Gonzalez, her stylist.

Thursday, 1 p.m.: Quick shopping stop

Thursday, 4 p.m.: Getting ready

It’s Ms. DeKreek’s favorite part of the day: getting ready. Tonight is “Greek wedding,” an annual tradition in which sororities and fraternities stage mock weddings between seniors, complete with funny speeches and parties.

Ms. DeKreek has never had a boyfriend. Though she eventually wants a family, she describes college hookup culture and setup dates as “a waste of time.”

“I just want to focus on myself,” she said, “and the right one will come along at some point.”

It’s a common sentiment among young women, who research indicates are having fewer romantic relationships than past generations.

Nearly three hours after starting to get ready, she heads to Ms. Gorham’s room to finish. It’s crowded with girls in long black dresses and small designer purses, smoothing, spraying, adjusting, asking to borrow one another’s heels.

“Cute!” they compliment one another. “Cute, cute, cute!”

Friday, 1 p.m.: Monthly facial

Saturday, 10 a.m.: Getting ready for Game Day

After an hour of curling her hair, Ms. DeKreek and her roommate deftly paint, blend, dab, brush, spray and dry their faces. Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Christina Aguilera sing from a speaker. Friends burst in without knocking to rummage through their wardrobes, needing to borrow cutoffs or jewelry.

This is what she means when she says, tenderly, “It’s like girlhood, all of us together.” She loves getting ready so much, she says, she sometimes doesn’t even feel like going out after.

Thinking about how others see her, after all, is “just kind of a dead end,” she said. “I’ve only found fulfillment through taking care of myself.”

If it seems paradoxical to find inner fulfillment through outer enhancement, well, that’s the promise society has held out to women since long before she was born.

She slides on a strapless gingham-and-lace minidress. The others are ready, all of them clomping around in tan knee-high boots, but she’s still dabbing and brushing. She unpins her curls, releasing bombshell cascades. Golden bangles click over her wrists. Before the mirror, she turns this way and that, all alone as a din of voices rises outside the door.

item.title: Woman Who Reported Assault Accuses University of Violating Consumer Law
item.description:
A former student who was sexually assaulted at Texas Christian University is suing the school using an unusual legal strategy, claiming it violated a consumer protection law in another state.

Sexual assault lawsuits against universities are difficult to win, often requiring proof that the universities acted with “deliberate indifference,” according to KC Johnson, a Brooklyn College professor who has studied lawsuits filed under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act.

As a result, plaintiffs have tried workarounds over the years. Even so, Dr. Johnson described a consumer protection claim as “highly unusual,” if not novel.

The lawsuit says T.C.U., a private university in Fort Worth, Texas, violated the Virginia Consumer Protection Act by misleading the woman, a Virginia resident, about the safety of its campus.

If successful, the lawsuit, brought by a woman identified only as Jane Doe, could broaden legal avenues for students frustrated with the outcomes of their complaints.

T.C.U. has argued that it does supply “services” in Virginia and that the woman wouldn’t have a complaint against T.C.U. if she had not attended school in Texas, asking that the case be dismissed or transferred to Texas.

Rulings on those questions are pending in a Virginia federal court.

In a statement, the university said it strongly disputed the lawsuit’s allegations and said the Virginia Consumer Protection Act claim “lacks legal and factual merit.”

The lawsuit claims the university’s recruiting practices are deceptive, but in its statement, T.C.U. said that information on campus crime statistics, including sex crimes, is made public and is available to prospective students.

The complainant has a powerful ally in Jay Jones, the Virginia attorney general, whose office wants the court to consider his brief in the case, arguing that the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, adopted to protect the state’s residents from fraudulent vendors, applies to out-of-state entities.

The attorney general’s office wrote that the law is clear: “Its prohibitions and protections extend beyond the borders of the commonwealth.”

The young woman at the center of the case attended high school in Virginia and, according to her lawsuit, was attracted to T.C.U. by a scholarship as well as the university’s representation that its campus was a safe place for women, the lawsuit said.

Her lawsuit said that she and her male assailant were at a party in fall 2024, her freshman year, where they both had alcoholic drinks.

After sharing an Uber back to the dorm where they both lived, the two made out in Ms. Doe’s bed for about 30 minutes until the male student left to go to the bathroom.

The woman fell asleep. She woke up to find the male student having sexual intercourse with her without a condom, the lawsuit said. It was an outcome she says she had neither consented to nor wanted, according to the lawsuit. She ordered him to leave.

The next day, the woman asked the student to meet and surreptitiously recorded him with her phone. In the recording, he admitted he had penetrated her without first seeking verbal consent, the documents said.

Following a hearing, a university panel concluded that the young man was guilty of sexual assault because he had sexual intercourse without consent.

The panel placed him on probation, ordered him to change dorms, required him to watch video trainings about “mutual consent,” and to write a paper of reflection.

Unsatisfied with his punishment, the woman submitted an appeal to the panel.

“The term nonconsensual sexual intercourse sounds so benign. But let’s call it what it is. In almost every state in America, nonconsensual sexual intercourse is rape,” she wrote.

“And what is the punishment for rape at T.C.U., according to the panel members? The punishment is homework!”

Following her appeal, the panel did not change its punishment.

After Ms. Doe’s lawyer sent T.C.U. a letter laying out what he viewed as its failures in the case, the university’s leadership overturned the panel’s decision, calling it inappropriate, and ordered the student suspended for two semesters.

By that time, the school year had ended and the young woman had left the T.C.U. campus for good.

The male student was not identified in the documents and could not be reached for comment.

The lawsuit argues that T.C.U.’s policies encourage rape. “Male students at T.C.U. know that nothing will happen to them for raping T.C.U.’s female students,” it said.

Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice for the National Women’s Law Center, said that, like Jane Doe, many women had been unhappy with how universities responded to their complaints, noting that the Trump administration had weakened regulations governing Title IX.

“I think its important to hold educational institutions accountable for what their promises are to students and their families when students are choosing to attend,” she said. “It wasn’t the safe place she assumed it would be.”

Ms. Doe’s lawyer, Thomas M. Wolf, argues the case is simple, saying, “Why would they be treated any differently from another vendor who misleads a Virginia consumer?”

item.title: How the ‘Manosphere’ Escaped the Internet and Invaded Conservative Colleges
item.description:
Should women have the right to vote? Should they work outside the home? Are they as smart as men? For years, those questions found audiences primarily in the extreme online world of the “manosphere,” where influencers get clicks by answering: “no.” Today, their formerly fringe ideas have escaped the dark recesses of social media and are gaining support in the real world, including (but not only) at elite religious and conservative colleges.

At Hillsdale, a selective, conservative liberal arts college in Michigan, a student wrote in the campus newspaper, “Three ugly words have wormed their way through campus, into Saturday-night conversations, laughter in the hallways and serious discussions: Repeal the 19th.” Another student noted that she had “heard several women seriously argue that women are intellectually and creatively deficient compared to men.”

Abigail Favale, a professor at the University of Notre Dame, recently told me that she has also seen “a real turn toward rigid gender roles and hierarchy” on campus, as increasing numbers of female students feel pressured by their peers and social media to picture themselves primarily as wives and mothers after graduation. Dr. Favale said she encountered some young women in “a state of dissonance,” torn between this view of strict gender roles and their own professional or academic goals.

Conservative think tanks, elected officials and the Republican Party itself have all struggled to offer a comprehensive response to the rise of this ideology, which I’ll call radical anti-feminism. Politicians have refused to acknowledge just how troubling these ideas are; some, such as Pete Hegseth, are elevating them. As a conservative myself, the most charitable interpretation I can think of for the general silence is that leaders are afraid that acknowledging such radical ideas, even to counter them, will offer them legitimacy. But some may believe that it’s in their interest to play footsie with this movement to woo more alienated young men to the Republican camp.

That is a serious moral and strategic error. Gen Z men swung almost 40 percentage points toward Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections, according to preliminary data from Times Voter Trends. There is no evidence that antifeminist rhetoric is capable of igniting sustained or pragmatic political engagement. Republicans also lost a 10-point advantage among white women and saw young women in general swing 28 points to the left, meaning the party has a lot of ground to make up with female voters if it hopes for success in the next presidential and congressional elections.

Combating radical antifeminism is not only good politics — it is the right thing to do. But tackling the problem requires explicitly recognizing its existence, offering a vigorous and vibrant counterargument and distinguishing it from other, legitimate debates over gender.

Conservatives get a lot right in our conversations about men and women. Biological differences between the sexes (especially concerning pregnancy and childbirth) are acknowledged, as are the real and sometimes irreconcilable tensions between work and home life. The right also tends to take seriously the unique problems facing boys and men right now: lower educational attainment, trouble finding good jobs, substance abuse problems and increased social alienation. I understand why young men who are struggling might be drawn to a vision of the world where there is a clear villain to blame.

A healthy conservatism leaves a lot of room for debate over what exactly is at the root of young men’s troubles and how best to help them. The conservative writer Helen Andrews, for example, has proposed that when women entered fields like academia and journalism in large numbers, they brought “feminine patterns of behavior” with them, alienating and disadvantaging men. I have repeatedly written in opposition to this “great feminization” thesis but it’s fair game for discussion.

But the ideas that women should not have the right to vote, that women are intellectually inferior to men, that women should not work? None of those would solve young men’s problems. And if conservatives treat those ideas as fodder for legitimate debate, it would only backfire on them and the young men they want to help.

Our economy and government cannot function without the extensive participation of American women. This should go without saying in 2026. As the midterm elections helped demonstrate, anyone who tries to turn that train around is going to get flattened.

What’s more, while radical antifeminists may pitch their philosophy as “traditional,” their ideas are far from it. My own great-great-grandmother worked as a clerk in the early 20th century after her husband died, so she could feed their young children. My great-grandmother, my grandmother, my mother and I have all worked, each of us scaling our careers up and down around family needs at times. Radical antifeminists ignore this reality, imagining an idealized past that never existed. (It should tell us something that a substantial amount of the visual imagery swirling around this phenomenon is A.I. generated.)

Tacitly tolerating this ideology is also backfiring on a social level. For mainstream conservatives who want young men and women to thrive, find meaning in life and build families, consider this: Radical antifeminism is making it difficult for some young conservatives in college to date. I have heard repeatedly about how its spread on campuses is killing off potential romances, as both sexes are increasingly suspicious of each other. Women don’t want to date men who see them as “lesser,” while men have been taught by the “manosphere” that women are untrustworthy and out to use them for money.

Without exaggerating its spread or influence, the trend is real and growing. But it also offers an opportunity for conservatives to come together around an agenda that actually does address the problems young men and women face. That will involve a real, substantive, even messy debate. But stripping women of the right to vote should not be on the table, nor should be relegating women to the kitchen. Those on the right contemplating a post-Trump future in 2028 and beyond should not want a movement in which the elite of the next generation is formed, even if only partially or indirectly, by misogyny. Conservatives must provide a better vision for the roles of young men and women — one that seeks out and inspires the best in both sexes.

Ivana Greco is a senior fellow at Capita, a nonpartisan think tank focused on family policy. She writes the newsletter The Home Front.

item.title: Philip Roth’s Lessons Arrived When I Needed Them Most
item.description:
As part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism, Times Opinion asked writers to revisit previously published articles. In 2013, Philip Roth wrote about his friendship with his former homeroom teacher. Below, Mr. Foer annotates Mr. Roth’s essay.

Tap a highlighted portion below to show or hide the annotations.

“In Memory of a Friend, Teacher and Mentor,” Philip Roth (2013)

I was 12 years old when I entered the Hawthorne Avenue Annex in February 1946. The Annex, a 15-minute bus ride for me from the main high school, was where you went in those days as a freshman at Newark’s Weequahic High. The first teacher I had to face on the first hour of my first day at the Annex was Bob Lowenstein. Dr. Lowenstein. Doc Lowenstein. He was fresh from serving in World War II, unlike most high school teachers he was unassumingly in possession of a Ph.D., and what was recognizable even to a 12-year-old was that this was a formidable man who did not gladly suffer fools.

Bob was my homeroom teacher. This meant that I saw him first thing in the morning, every single day of the school year. I was never to take a language course with him — I had Mademoiselle Glucksman for French and Señorita Baleroso for Spanish — but I didn’t forget him. Who at Weequahic did? Consequently, when it came his turn to be mauled in Congress’s anti-Communist crusade of the 1940s and 1950s, I followed his fate as best I could in the stories that I had my parents clip from the Newark newspapers and mail to me.

I don’t remember how we came together again around 1990, about 40 years after I’d graduated Weequahic High. I was back in America from having lived largely abroad for some 12 years, and either I wrote to him about something or he wrote to me about something and we met for lunch at Zelda and his house in West Orange. In the spirit of Bob Lowenstein, I will put the matter in plain language, directly as I can: I believe we fell in love with each other.

He sent me his poems in the mail, sometimes as soon as he’d finished writing them, and I sent him my books when they were published. I even sent him the final draft of one book — “American Pastoral” — to read in manuscript. There was lots in the book about early-20th-century Newark, and I wanted to pass it before him to make sure I’d got everything right.

I sent someone down to West Orange to drive Bob the two and a half hours up to my house in rural northwest Connecticut, and together the two of us had lunch and I asked him to tell me what he’d made of what I’d written. We talked over lunch — we talked all afternoon long. He had, as usual, a lot to say, and I believe I listened to all that he said no less attentively than I listened in that 8:30 homeroom at the Hawthorne Avenue Annex when he read out the announcements for the school day.

In “I Married a Communist,” the narrator Nathan Zuckerman says, “I think of my life as one long speech that I’ve been listening to.” For me, Bob’s is one of the persuasive voices I can still hear speaking. The tang of the real permeated his talk. Like all great teachers, he personified the drama of transformation through talk.

I should mention that when he arrived at my Connecticut house from West Orange, he got out of the car with a book in his hand. What he’d been reading on the drive up were the poems, in French, written by the French Catholic poet Charles Péguy during the course of a brief life that ended almost a hundred years ago. I knew, of course, that Bob was a serious man, but only when I saw that he took Péguy to read on the road did I realize just how serious.

In 1993, when I turned 60, I gave a reading in South Orange, at Seton Hall University, and the reading’s sponsors threw me a little birthday party afterward. Bob and Zelda were there. In fact, my reading that night was introduced by Bob, who, as you recall, lived a mile away from Seton Hall and never missed a poetry reading there. He was then 85. That he had 20 more years of sparkling life left in him — well, who could have known that, except perhaps Bob himself?

I had written to ask him to introduce me, and seeing him up at the Seton Hall lectern that night recounting with great wit and sharpness and charm our first acquaintance as pupil and student made me inordinately happy. I believe it made him happy too.

Bob was the model for a major figure in my novel “I Married a Communist,” a book I published in 1998 recalling the anti-Communist period I mentioned earlier and that savage, malicious mauling that people like Bob suffered in those years from the teeth and the claws of the scum then in power.

The character is a retired high school teacher named Murray Ringold, and, like Bob, he teaches at Weequahic High, though not, like Bob, Romance languages but English. I also altered Bob’s appearance, his war record and certain significant details of his personal life — Bob didn’t, for example, have a hotheaded murderer for a brother — but otherwise I tried to remain true to the force of his virtues, as I perceived them.

I also included in passing his singular pleasure of hurling a blackboard eraser when what was said by a pupil seemed to him radically knuckleheaded and more than likely the oafish outgrowth of inattentiveness, the crime of crimes.

The subject of “I Married a Communist” is, at bottom, education, tutelage, mentorship, in particular the education of an eager, earnest and impressionable adolescent in how to become — as well as how not to become — a bold and honorable and effective man. This is no easy task, as we know, for there are two large stumbling blocks: the impurity of the world and the impurity of oneself, not to mention one’s massive imperfections of intelligence, emotion, foresight and judgment.

This book about a boy and his men opens with a brief portrait of Murray Ringold, the Ringold brother who is not violent and whose rage is tempered and reserved for unwarrantable injustice. Murray Ringold, by the way, undergoes an education of his own. So too did Bob, of course, when, impaled suddenly on his moment in time, caught in the trap set to ruin so many promising careers of that American era — a casualty like thousands of others of the first shameful decade in his country’s postwar history — he was forced for six years out of the Newark school system and his chosen profession, expelled as a political deviant and a dangerous man to let loose on the young.

I refer now not to a boy’s but to an adult’s education: in loss, grief and, that inescapable component of living, betrayal. Bob had iron in him and he resisted the outrage of the injustice with extraordinary courage and bravery, but he was a man, and he felt it as a man, and so he suffered too.

I hope that in my novel I have given ample recognition to the qualities of our late, legendary and noble friend, who understood, as did the poet Charles Péguy, that “tyranny is always better organized than freedom.” I don’t know how Péguy found this out, but Bob learned it the hard way.

item.title: Influencer University
item.description:
Good morning! Want to be an influencer? While I don’t think I have the stamina, I love watching the vlogs.

My colleague spent time with Haley DeKreek, a junior at the University of Arizona and member of the Alpha Phi sorority, who has more than 45,000 TikTok followers. She’s part of a boom of sorority content known as #RushTok.

Her chosen career path? Influencing. She’s in good company. A recent survey found that nearly four in 10 Gen Z respondents said they would take a million social media followers over a steady 9-to-5 job.

In the days before a homecoming game, Haley’s schedule was packed as she went from beauty appointment to beauty appointment. “I love being a girl,” she said.

Go inside the life of a sorority influencer.

We’re also covering:

Data centers

The next James Bond

International students

What to discuss in class today.

1. A winter nightmare is looming in Ukraine. Russia has opened a bombing campaign that is intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation.

2. Did a routine router upgrade lead to a U.S. ground stop? Officials thought that a facility in Arkansas was remote enough that they could do the upgrade work without much harm. The underlying cause is unclear. Here’s what we know.

3. President Trump is expected to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, this week. The fallout from the Nvidia scandal is hanging over the meeting.

4. Congress is debating a bill that would charge data centers billions. It could make it easier to build data centers for A.I., but those centers would have to pay extra for access to the electric grid.

5. Raye is the top Grammy nominee. She tied a record Beyoncé set at the 2025 ceremony for most nominations for a female artist. Here’s a list of the nominees.

6. The next James Bond is … Robert Pattinson. The English actor succeeds Daniel Craig to become the seventh person to play the superspy.

7. Look up tonight. The Leonids meteor shower is peaking. It’s best seen from the Northern Hemisphere.

The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s chancellor tried to protect the school from the wrath of the Trump administration. Work on cancer, suicide, AIDS and coronaviruses was sacrificed anyway. Here’s how.

Trump administration policies appear to be scaring away international students for a second year. A survey released today found that new international student enrollment at American universities plunged by 15 percent.

Student loan caps are complicating the dreams of some aspiring doctors, who are entering medical school with limits on how much they can borrow.

A former student who was sexually assaulted at Texas Christian University is suing the school. She’s using an unusual legal strategy, claiming that the university violated a consumer protection law in another state.

Trisha Paytas spoke at Harvard Business School.

Joe Rogan weighed in on the midterms. After relative silence, Rogan said that Trump’s policies had lost “the podcast bros.”

Maybe it’s a flop? Maybelline debuted its first new tag line in more than three decades. Some. People. Are. Confused.

Billy Evans said he would do it all over again. Evans, the partner of Elizabeth Holmes, said in a CBS interview that he would “100 percent” make “You Can See Everything” once more. Here are five takeaways.

“S.N.L.” brought back Bowen Yang. He returned to play the former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in a cold open with a gaggle of tech giants. Read our recap.

AO3, the fan fiction site, is back. The archive was taken down more than two weeks ago in a “security incident,” leaving its 12 million users in shock.

Do this to get ahead.

Laugh at yourself. Experts say it could help other people feel more at ease around you.

Strengthen your muscles. I’m finally working out again, and I need to start lifting more weights. These five muscles are important to prioritize as you get older.

Make some cookies. These are the best ready-to-bake chocolate chip cookie doughs.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Harrison Hill and Hiroko Masuike were our photo editors.
